div.p: The Hierarchical Scheduling Framework (HSF) has been introduced as a design-time framework enabling compositional schedulability analysis of embedded software systems with real-time properties. However, supporting resource sharing in HSF is a major challenge, since it increases the amount of CPU resources required to guarantee schedulability of the hard real time tasks, and it decreases the composability at the system level. In this paper, we focus on a compositional framework called the bounded-delay resource open environment (BROE) server, and we identify key parameters of this framework that have a great effect on how the framework will utilize CPU resources. In addition, we show how to select optimal values for these parameters in order to reduce the required CPU resource.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The current trend in many software intensive industrial application domains, including automotive and avionics, is to integrate more software applications into a lower number of processors in order to reduce the cost of the system as well as the complexity of the network communication. Many of these applications have real-time requirements which raise the problem of guaranteeing the timing behavior of these applications after integrating them in a single processor. In addition integration requires a temporal isolation between the applications during run-time to prevent one application from causing a failure of another application.

The Hierarchical Scheduling Framework (HSF) provides means for decomposing a complex software system into well-defined parts called subsystems. It provides a mechanism for timing predictable composition of the integrated applications. It also provides temporal isolation between subsystems (applications) that are integrated into one processor. In the HSF a subsystem provides an introspective interface (real-time interface) that specifies the timing properties of the subsystem precisely. This means that each subsystem can be independently developed and tested, and later assembled without introducing unwanted temporal behavior. Finally, the HSF facilitates reusability of subsystems in timing-critical and resource constrained environments.

Earlier efforts have been made in supporting compositional subsystem integration in the HSFs, preserving the independently analyzed schedulability of individual subsystems. One of the common assumptions shared by earlier studies is that subsystems are independent. However, this assumption may not be valid since many industrial applications have to allow dependencies between applications in terms of sharing logical resources.

In this work, we target HSFs allowing for dependencies. Specifically, we explore generation of real-time interfaces for the recently-proposed bounded-delay resource open environment (BROE) compositional framework [9]. Current work has focused on determining subsystem schedulability and system composability given a real-time interface for each subsystem. However, no work addresses how such a real-time interface is determined for each subsystem. Our contributions in this area are:
• We discuss and identify the key parameters for realtime interface generation in BROE.
• We generalize the local scheduler for BROE by including the analysis for Fixed Priority preemptive Scheduling FPS.

• We show how to select the optimal interface that requires less CPU resource to obtain a high degree of composability. §Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 briefly reviews prior work on HSF. Section 3 describes the model and context of our work. Section 4 gives the reader a brief review of the BROE frame-work. Section 5 describes techniques for interface generation in BROE. Section 6 describes techniques for selecting the optimal interface among all possible BROE interfaces. Finally, Section 7 concludes with possible future work.

div.head: Related work
div.p: Over the years, there has been a growing research attention on real-time compositional models. Deng and Liu [12] proposed a two-level hierarchical scheduling framework for open systems, where subsystems may be developed and validated independently. Kuo and Li [16] presented schedulability analysis techniques for such a two-level framework with the FPS global scheduler. Lipari and Baruah [17,20] presented schedulability analysis techniques for Earliest Deadline First (EDF) global schedulers. Mok et al. [14,21] proposed the bounded-delay virtual processor model to achieve a clean separation in a multi-level HSF. In addition, Shin and Lee [23] introduced the periodic virtual processor model (to characterize the periodic CPU allocation behaviour), and many studies have been proposed on schedulability analysis with this model under FPS [2,10,18] and under EDF scheduling [23,24]. More recently, Easwaran et al. [13] introduced Explicit Deadline Periodic (EDP) virtual processor model. However, a common assumption shared by all above studies is that tasks are independent.

Recently, three SRP-based [3] synchronization protocols for inter-subsystem resource sharing have been presented, i.e., HSRP [11], BROE [9], and SIRAP [7]. A preliminary comparative assessment of these three synchronization protocols [6] revealed that none of them was superior to the others and that the performance of a protocol heavily depends on system parameters.

div.head: System model
div.p: We assume that each subsystem consist of a sporadic task system. A sporadic task τ i = (e i , d i , p i ) is characterized by a worst-case execution requirement e i , a (relative) deadline d i , and a minimum inter-arrival separation p i , which is, for historical reasons, also referred to as the period of the task. Such a sporadic task generates a potentially infinite sequence of jobs, with successive job-arrivals separated by at least p i time units. Each job has a worstcase execution requirement equal to e i and a deadline that occurs d i time units after its arrival time. A sporadic task system S k def = {τ 1 , . . . , τ n } is a collection of n such sporadic tasks. (Note we overload S k to refer to the subsystem and its contingent task system). We assume that the sporadic tasks are indexed in non-decreasing order of their relative deadline parameters: d i ≤ d i+1 (∀i). A useful metric for a sporadic task τ i is the task utilization u i def = e i /p i . The system utilization is denoted U (S k ) def = τi∈S k u i . Finally, we assume that jobs of a subsystem execute (hierarchically) within the virtual processor's allocation according to the earliest-deadline-first (EDF) and FPS (deadline monotonic) scheduling policy.

div.head: Stack-Resource Protocol (SRP)
div.p: The subsystem is assumed to execute upon a platform consisting of a single dedicated preemptive processor, and m other non-preemptable serially reusable resources R 1 , R 2 , . . . , R m . Let c i,j denote the length (in terms of WCET) of the largest critical section in τ i that holds resource R j .

For this paper, we consider that each subsystem arbitrates access to shared resources (either global or local) via the Stack Resource Policy (SRP) [3]. The subsystem maintains a value Π k (R j ) def = min{i | τ i accesses R j } called the resource ceiling for any resource R j . Whenever resource R j is locked by a task τ i only tasks with index strictly less than Π k (R j ) may preempt τ i . §Resource Hold-Time. In a compositional system, the duration of time during which one subsystem locks a resource -thus, preventing other subsystems from accessing the resource-has an effect on the schedulability of the overall system. To quantify the interference due to the locking of global resources, Fisher et al. [15] introduced the concept of resource hold-time. The resource hold-time is the maximum duration for which a resource is locked by some computational entity (e.g., task, subsystem, or system). To compute H k , we need to define and determine the following two parameters:
• h i,k (R ): the resource hold-time for task τ i ∈ S k on resource R . Section 5.1 will have more h i,k details.
• H k (R ): the subsystem resource hold-time for subsystem S k on resource R . The parameter H k (R ) can be determined from max τi∈S k {h i,k (R )}.
From the above parameters, the subsystem parameter H k can be determined as follows:
div.formula: H k def = max Rj ∈{R1,...,Rm} {H k (R j )}(1)

div.head: BROE compositional framework
div.p: The BROE server is similar to the constant bandwidth server (CBS) [1] with modifications for dealing with globally-shared, non-preemptible serially-reusable resources. A full description of the BROE server would require significant space and fortunately is not required to understand our results. For a complete description of BROE, the interested reader is directed to Bertogna et al. [9]. Instead, in this paper, we will simply describe some of the salient features of BROE. §BROE Real-Time Interface. In the bounded-delay resource open environment (BROE) compositional framework [9], each subsystem S k 's real-time interface is represented by a three-tuple (α k , Δ k , H k ). The first term α k represents the "fraction" of the processor's execution time that virtual processor executing subsystem S k receives over time. The second term Δ k represents the maximum execution jitter that subsystem S k experiences in processing time allocation. The H k term represents the maximum resource hold-time for S k ; that is, the maximum amount of time the S k can lock a global-shared resource and potentially block other subsystems from executing on the processing platform. From the real-time interface (α k , Δ k , H k ), we may determine some system parameters necessary to implement a virtual processor for BROE. The following parameter P k gives the virtual processor period and is determined as follows:
div.formula: P k def = Δ k 2(1 -α k )(2)
div.p: The virtual processor period specifies the time between when the budget of the virtual processor for S k is replenished. At a replenishment time, the budget is set to a value Q k . The budget is consumed as the virtual processor executes S k (at a rate of one unit of budget per unit of time executed). The virtual processor is not eligible to execute after the budget has expired (i.e., reached zero), until the next budget replenishment time. The value of Q k is determined as Q k def = α k P k Many researchers have observed that resource-sharing between subsystems is complicated if a subsystem's budget expires while it holds a lock on a globally-shared resource. The reason for this difficulty arises from the fact that the subsystem, with the expired budget holding the resource, may unnecessarily block other subsystems from obtaining the resource. BROE deals with this issue by checking at the time S k whether there is sufficient budget left to complete resource access before budget expiration. Since the resource hold-time parameter H k quantifies the maximum duration of a resource lock for subsystem S k , the virtual processor may simply check whether H k is less than the current budget at the time of S k 's global resource request. Therefore, the initial budget must be large enough to at least accommodate one resource access; i.e.,
div.formula: H k ≤ Q k (3
div.p: If there is not sufficient budget at the time of the resource request, the virtual processor for S k will prematurely expire the budget and proportionally move the next replenishment point forward (see [9] for details). Thus, BROE never permits budget expiration during an access to a globally-shared resource.

div.head: Interface generation for BROE
div.p: In this section, we discuss the problem of determining the virtual processor parameters given a subsystem S k . Ideally, the designer would simply (and efficiently) choose the parameters from some range of valid interface parameters that increase system composability while simultaneously ensuring subsystem schedulability. Unfortunately, determining the "best" parameters is not a simple choice as the composability of the system depends upon interface parameter chosen by other subsystems. Furthermore, the search space of parameters for a subsystem can be quite large. In [5] we have considered the problem of generating interfaces for a subsystem given the virtual processor period P k and the resource ceilings Π k (R ). In this paper, we take a further step and assume that the resources ceilings are not given and we will search for the optimal settings of resource ceiling to minimize the CPU requirements. Given the virtual processor period P k , we now address how the interface parameters are related and generated using an approach similar to the one presented in [22].

div.head: Optimal interface
div.p: In this section, we explain the problem of evaluating the optimal subsystem interfaces that require less CPU resource. (4) can be used as a measure of minimum amount of processor allocations necessary to guarantee the schedulability of the system and we refer to it as system load (load sys ) that is evaluated as follows,
div.formula: load sys = max ∀S ⎛ ⎝ max Sj:Pj >P {H j } P + S k :P k ≤P Q k P k ⎞ ⎠ .
div.p: (17) Given the definition of load sys , we aim at finding the optimal subsystem timing interfaces for all subsystems that decrease load sys . Looking at (17), the parameters that may affect load sys are Q k and H j (P k is given), and decreasing the values of these parameters can decrease load sys .

Moreover, evaluating the minimum subsystem budget Q k can be done using ( 16) for the given subsystem period P k and the resource ceilings. For H k , it can be decreased by artificially decreasing the resource ceilings of the global shared resources (the minimum value can be obtained when the ceiling of all resources equal to 1). Decreasing the resource ceiling of the global shared resources will decrease the interference from higher priority tasks (see (7)). However, decreasing the resource ceiling will increase the blocking (b k (L) and b in ( 13) and ( 10)) on the higher priority tasks that may in turn increase the minimum subsystem budget Q k required to guarantee the schedulability of the subsystem. That means decreasing H k may increase the minimum Q k and as a consequence we can not decide if decreasing H k can increase or decrease the systems load because H k affects higher priority subsystems while Q k affects the lower priority subsystems and the subsystem itself in (17). We can conclude that there is a tradeoff between decreasing the subsystem budget Q k and the resource holding time H k , and the optimal selection of the resource ceilings depend not only on the subsystem and its task parameters but also on the other subsystems parameters. However, the parameters of the other subsystems that will be integrated with the subsystem under development, may not be available.

The same observation has been reported by Shin et al. [22] for a solution for a simpler resource-sharing HSF system based on a two-step approach; where 1) in the first step, refered as interface candidate generation, a set of interface candidates are evaluated during the design of each subsystem, and 2) in the second step, called interface candidate selection, the optimal interface candidate for each subsystem is selected during the integration phase. In this section, we show how a similar two-step approach can be used for the systems that use BROE.

div.head: Interface candidate generation
div.p: The problem of interface candidate generation can be formulated as follows; given a subsystem S k , global shared resources, and the subsystem period, we find all possible subsystem timing interfaces, including the minimum subsystem bandwidth and the resource holding time, that have a potential to constitutes an optimal solution to system load. Note that, the subsystem bandwidth can be changed only when changing the subsystem budget Q k , as the subsystem period P k is given (fixed value) so we can use Q k in the subsystem interface instead of α k , for the same reasoning,
div.formula: Q k can be used instead of Δ k since Δ k = 2P k -2Q k .
div.p: As a results, an interface candidate that includes the parameters that can be changed is denoted as (Q k,j , H k,j ) where j indicates interface candidate index.
div.formula: Definition 1 An interface candidate (Q k,j , H k,j ) is said to be redundant if there exists (Q k,i , H k,i ) such that H k,i ≤ H k,j and Q k,i ≤ Q k,j , where j < i (denoted as (Q k,i , H k,i ) ≤ (Q k,j , H k,j )). In addition, (Q k,i , H k,i ) is said to be non-redundant if it is not redundant. Lemma 2 If (Q k , H k ) ≤ (Q * k , H * k ), (Q k , H k ) will never contribute more to load sys than (Q * k , H * k ) does.
div.p: Proof Form the definition of redundant interface, using a redundant candidate may increases the sum part for the lower priority subsystems and the blocking H j for the higher priority subsystems in ( 17) compared with nonredundant interface. That is, a redundant candidate only has a potential to increase load sys .

Based on Lemma 2 we can exclude all redundant candidates from a solution and only the set of interface candidates that have potential to constitute an optimal solution to system load, should be considered.

Looking at (5) and ( 6), the resource holding time h i,k (R ) may change depending on Q k and Π(R ), and the other parameters have fixed values (P k , pj, c i,j ). For the case when P k < p min , (8) can be used to evaluate the resource holding time, which makes the problem of evaluating non-redundant interface candidate easier. The reason is that using (8), then the value of resource holding time of R can be changed only if we change the resource ceiling Π(R ).
In this paper, we focus on the case when P k ≤ p min , and leave the general case (P k > p min ) as a future work.

However, the same result holds for BROE, but because of the space limit, we show that the properties of the system load, subsystem budget and resource holding time equations that the prove in [22] is based on, are also similar for BROE.

div.head: Interface selection
div.p: In the previous section, we have shown how to evaluate a set of non-redundant interfaces for each subsystem, in this section we show how to select a system configuration consisting of one interface from each subsystem that minimize the system load. We use the ICS algorithm (Figure 2) presented in [22] and we show that it is also applicable with BROE.

Before applying the ICS algorithm, the set of interface candidates (Q k , H k ), for each subsystem, should be sorted in a decreasing order of H k . Since the set of interface candidates does not contain any redundant candidate then it follows that (after sorting the set based on H k ) each set is sorted in an increasing order of subsystem budget (Q k ). That means the first candidate (Q k,1 , H k,1 ) has the largest resource holding time and the smallest subsystem budget.

The ICS algorithm generates a finite number of system configurations through iteration steps. Each configuration is a set of individual interface candidates of all subsystems. Let CF i denote a configuration that ICS generates at an i-th iteration step. For notational convenience, we introduce a variable f i k to denote an element of CF i , i.e.,
div.formula: CF i = {f i 1 , . . . , f i N }. The variable f i k represents the inter- face candidate index of a subsystem S k , indicating that the configuration in the i-th step includes (Q k,f i k , H k,f i k ). Initialization.
div.p: In the beginning, this algorithm generates an initial configuration CF 0 which contains the first interface candidates of all subsystems i.e., CF 0 = {1, . . . , 1}. Iteration step. The ICS algorithm transits from (i -1)-th step to i-th step, increasing by one only the index f i k * of a subsystem S k * in CF i-1 that may decrease the load sys . To find S k * , first the algorithm finds the subsystem S s * , in line 5 of Figure 2, that cause the maximum value in (17), i.e., the value of load sys . Then it finds the index of the subsystem that imposes the largest blocking to the subsystem S s * in line 6. This can easily be found from the inner max function in (17) and assuming S = S s * , i.e., k * = a : H a = max Sj :Pj >P {H j }. Increasing the index of subsystem S k * decreases H k * which decreases the blocking imposed to S s * that cause maximum function which decreases it. At the same time Q k * is increased which may affect the system load value.

When such S k * is found, it then checks whether the H k * can be further reduced (in line 7 of Figure 2). If so, it is reduced (in line 8), and CF i-1 becomes to CF i (in line 9). Iteration termination. The above iteration process terminates when the blocking from H k * to subsystem S s * cannot be reduced further. The algorithm then finds the smallest value of load sys out of the values saved during the iteration, and it returns a set of interfaces corresponding to the smallest value. Complexity of the algorithm. During an i-th iteration, the algorithm only increases the interface candidate index of a subsystem S k * . Then, it can repeat O(N * m ) iterations, where N is the number of subsystems and m is the greatest number of interface candidates of a subsystem among all.

We now show that the optimal configuration must be included in the set of the configurations that the ICS algorithm generates. This will show the optimality of our algorithm. The proof is nearly identical to [22] and is divided into two parts; the first part is based on the system load analysis and the second part is based on the algorithm itself including the initialization, iteration and termination. Since we are using the same algorithm then we need to focus only on the system load part.
Using BROE and by the definition of s * , we can reduce the value of load sys (i -1) (at step i -1) by either reducing the maximum blocking H k * in (17) and/or by reducing the summation part in (17)

div.p: A key aspect of this algorithm is that it always reduces the blocking part, but does not reduce the subsystem budget in the summation part. An intuition behind this is as follows: the algorithm starts from the interface candidates that have the smallest subsystem budget but the largest resource holding times, respectively. Hence, for each interface candidate, there is no room to further reduce the summation part of (17). However, there is a chance to reduce the maximum blocking H k * imposed to S s * .

Based on this it can be proved that at any transition from step i -1 to i that increasing any index of a subsystem in CF i-1 other than the one that the algorithm increases will never decrease the system load. In addition, when the algorithm terminates, it is not possible to decrease the system load by increasing the index of any subsystem in CF i-1 .

div.head: Future work & conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we have presented the first known analysis assuming FPS local scheduler for BORE server. In addition, we have shown how the two-step approach and its associated algorithms proposed in [22] can be used with BROE under assumption that the subsystem period is given and it is less than the shortest task period of all tasks that belong to that server. The ICG algorithm will not be able to find all non-redundant interface candidates if we relax the above assumption (subsystem period is less than the shortest task period). The reason is that we should use ( 5) and ( 6) to evaluate the resource holding time and that makes the resource holding time dependent on the subsystem budget which will increase the complexity of the analysis. Currently, we are developing an algorithm that can find all non-redundant interface candidates independent on the task and subsystem periods.
